subtype: Approach: setting a goal with an amount and date [Thinking]
passage: Note from Vidya, class teacher. Ojas stayed after maths with a folded paper. He wants a secondhand bicycle that costs 4,000 rupees and has given himself six months. “That's a lot,” he said, and I stayed quiet. He counted aloud: “Six months is about twenty-six weeks. 4,000 divided by 26 is about 155 a week. My allowance is 200 a week. So I'd still have 45 for snacks.” He laughed, surprised. “It's not as big as it sounded.” He wrote the target date at the top of the page and the weekly figure beside it. I asked only whether he would tell his parents, and he said tonight. I will ask him about it in a month.

qa.q: How much does the secondhand bicycle cost?
qa.a: The bicycle costs 4,000 rupees.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he finished counting?
qa.a: Ojas felt surprised and encouraged, since he laughed and said it was not as big as it sounded.

qa.q: What could Ojas do if a week's saving falls short?
qa.a: He could move the date a little or earn small extra money, since a fixed weekly figure with some slack keeps the goal alive.

qa.q: How might Ojas's parents feel when he tells them the plan tonight?
qa.a: They may feel pleased and proud that Ojas worked out the numbers himself, and more willing to back the goal.

grounding: A teen turns a bicycle price and a six-month deadline into a weekly saving figure and finds it more realistic than he thought.

passage: Monday was allowance day, and at the school's savings-club table Irfan sir was already counting envelopes. Yamini took her 400 rupees from her bag, counted out a fifth, 80 rupees, and slid it into her envelope marked TRIP. Irfan sir wrote her name in the register. “Before the canteen?” he asked. “Before anything,” Yamini said. “If I wait for leftovers, there aren't any.” Last month she had promised herself she would save whatever remained on Friday, and found only coins. She tucked the rest into her wallet and walked to the canteen with 320 in her hand, and it felt like plenty.

qa.q: How much did Yamini put into her envelope?
qa.a: Yamini counted out a fifth, 80 rupees, and slid it into her envelope.

qa.q: What does Yamini's remark about leftovers suggest she felt after last month?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated with herself, since she had promised to save what remained and found only coins.

qa.q: What could Yamini do if the fixed amount feels too tight some weeks?
qa.a: She could lower the fixed portion a little but still set it aside first, since saving first keeps the habit steady.

qa.q: How might Irfan sir see Yamini's choice?
qa.a: Irfan sir may feel pleased to see a student set money aside before spending, since he asked about the canteen and wrote her name in the register.

grounding: On the day the allowance arrives, a student sets aside a fixed portion before spending, so saving does not depend on leftovers.

subtype: Approach: tracking spending and finding leaks [Action]
passage: Tiny notebook, blue cover. That's the whole secret, Jatin. For one month I wrote down everything I bought, even the five-rupee stuff, and I did not judge myself. On the last day I added it up and my stomach dropped: chips, sweets and phone recharges together were about a third of my money. I had no idea. I always thought it was clothes, or that one birthday gift. Nobody told me to stop. I just looked at the page and decided, this is a lot for chips and data I barely use. So I made two changes: treats only on Fridays, and a smaller recharge plan. I didn't cut everything, because I like a samosa. I'm Usha, the only girl in class with a ledger, and Mum calls me her little accountant. I'm still eating samosas.

qa.q: What share of Usha's money did chips, sweets and phone recharges take?
qa.a: Chips, sweets and phone recharges together were about a third of Usha's money.

qa.q: What did Usha feel when she added up the month?
qa.a: Usha felt shocked, since her stomach dropped and she had no idea where so much had gone.

qa.q: What could Usha add to keep the savings going?
qa.a: She could set a weekly limit for treats and recharges and keep noting purchases, since the notebook showed exactly where the money leaked.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Jatin may feel curious and even inspired to try a notebook, since the tone is light and Usha is not lecturing.

grounding: A teen writes down every purchase for a month, finds snacks and top-ups take a third of her money and trims those two areas by choice.

subtype: Approach: earning extra through small honest work [Action]
passage: Note from Kamal, Leela's father. Leela came to me on Sunday with a plan: teach maths to two younger children in our building for 50 rupees a session, twice a week. She asked me first whether it was allowed, and asked me to speak to their parents, which I did. The lessons happen at our dining table, with me in the next room. She prepares worksheets on Sunday night, which I never asked for. Half of what she earns goes into the tin for her secondhand bicycle. She showed me the sums: her target date has moved from December to October, and she is pleased but tired on Wednesdays. I have told her that school work comes first, and we will review it in a month.

qa.q: How much does Leela charge for each session?
qa.a: Leela charges 50 rupees a session.

qa.q: What is Leela feeling about the extra work, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She is pleased but a little tired, since she proudly shows the sums with the date moved earlier, yet she is tired on Wednesdays.

qa.q: What could Leela do if the tutoring gets too tiring?
qa.a: She could cut to one session a week or trim some spending, since the goal should not cost her school work.

qa.q: How might the children's parents see the tutoring?
qa.a: They may feel glad to have a trusted older neighbour helping their children for a small fee, especially since Kamal spoke to them first.

grounding: A student offers small honest tutoring after checking with parents and puts part of the earnings toward the same goal, speeding it up.

subtype: Approach: spending impulsively at the first temptation [Pitfall]
passage:
“Pranav, why is there a shoebox on your bed?” Rekha didi asked.
“Sale. Half price. It ended in an hour, so I just bought them.”
“With what money?”
“The bicycle money.” He nudged the box with his foot. “But they're really good shoes.”
“How much was in the tin?”
“Three thousand one hundred. Now it's two thousand one hundred. Wait.” He counted on his fingers. “That's two more months of saving, isn't it?”
“At your weekly amount, yes. Two months.”
“I didn't even need them. Mine are fine.”
“What would have happened if you'd waited a day?”
“I'd have looked at the tin and not clicked buy.”
“Then stick a note on the tin: sleep on it before buying.”
Pranav groaned, then reached for a pen.

qa.q: How much money is left in the tin?
qa.a: Two thousand one hundred is left in the tin.

qa.q: What is Pranav feeling as he counts on his fingers?
qa.a: Pranav feels regretful and a little sheepish, since he admits he didn't even need the shoes.

qa.q: What could Pranav do to stop impulse buys in future?
qa.a: He could sleep on it for a day before buying, as the note on the tin says, since the urge fades and the goal stays in sight.

qa.q: How might Rekha didi feel about the purchase?
qa.a: Rekha may feel concerned yet supportive, since she asks questions instead of scolding and offers a simple note rule.

grounding: A teen with saved money buys shoes on impulse at an online sale, and the bicycle goal is set back by two months.

passage:
“Akash, you getting the cheese sandwich and the shake again?” Gargi asked, holding her tray.
“Everyone's getting it. It would look weird if I just had a samosa.”
“That's about a hundred a day.”
“I know. It's the 28th.” He stared into his wallet. “I've got 140 rupees left for the rest of the month.”
“What were you saving for?”
“A proper football. I wanted it by now.”
“And?”
“Not even close.” He put the shake back in the fridge. “Maybe I'll have the samosa. What will they say?”
“I think Manav only buys it because Dev does. Everyone's copying someone.”
Akash laughed, a little embarrassed. “Okay. Samosa and tea. If they laugh, I'll survive.”

qa.q: How much money does Akash have left for the rest of the month?
qa.a: Akash has 140 rupees left for the rest of the month.

qa.q: Why did Akash keep buying the cheese sandwich and the shake?
qa.a: He was afraid of feeling left out, since it would look weird to have only a samosa, so he wanted to fit in with his classmates.

qa.q: What could Akash try with his friends instead?
qa.a: He could set a small treat budget and still join them with something cheaper, since he can stay part of the group while protecting the football fund.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Akash's spending?
qa.a: Gargi seems concerned but friendly, since she asks what he was saving for without judging and points out that everyone is copying someone.

grounding: A student buys expensive treats to match classmates at the canteen and finds at month end that little remains for what he wanted.

subtype: Approach: making saving visible with a chart [Action]
passage:
“Bhavna, what is that red tube on your wall?” Mummy asked.
“A savings thermometer. The top is 3,000 for the camera, and each section is 250. See? I coloured the first two.”
“You could just check your tin.”
“The tin is boring. I need to see it going up. Last week I wanted earrings, and then I looked at the wall and thought, that's one box I won't colour.”
“So it's working?”
“Two boxes done, ten to go. I skipped pizza tonight, and my hand is itching to colour box three.”
From the kitchen Papa called, “Jaya, is the dal ready?” Mummy laughed. “Give me the red pen. I'll hold the tape.”

qa.q: How much is each section of the thermometer worth?
qa.a: Each section is 250.

qa.q: What does Bhavna feel when she wants earrings and looks at the wall?
qa.a: She feels tempted but determined, because the thought of one box she won't colour keeps her going.

qa.q: What could Bhavna do if the chart stops motivating her?
qa.a: She could add a small reward at each milestone or tell the family so they can cheer her on, since visible progress helps through dull weeks.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the thermometer?
qa.a: Mummy seems amused and supportive, since she asks for the pen and offers to hold the tape, and she sees her daughter's effort.

grounding: A teen draws a savings thermometer on her wall and colours it each week, and seeing it fill keeps her saving through tempting weeks.

subtype: Approach: falling for easy-money schemes online [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Gurleen, and for twenty minutes I was sure I was a genius. Minakshi showed me an ad in a game: send 1,500 rupees, get 3,000 back in a week, no risk. I had exactly that saved from two years of allowance. I was already spending the extra 1,500 in my head, a new bag, treats for my cousins. My thumb was over the send button when Mummy walked in and asked why I looked so pale. I showed her the phone. She didn't shout. She said offers that double your money in days are almost always frauds, and that if the money were real, nobody would need to advertise it in a game. We closed it, and she showed me how to report the ad. I felt silly, then relieved.

qa.q: How much did the ad ask Gurleen to send?
qa.a: The ad asked Gurleen to send 1,500 rupees.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling while imagining the extra money, and afterwards?
qa.a: Gurleen felt excited and sure of being a genius, and afterwards felt silly and then relieved.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do the next time an offer promises fast money?
qa.a: Gurleen could show it to a parent or another adult first, since a promise of doubled money in days is a warning sign.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when she saw the phone?
qa.a: Mummy was probably worried and protective, yet stayed calm, since she didn't shout but explained and helped report the ad.

grounding: A teen imagines quick success from an online promise to double savings and nearly sends money before a parent explains it is likely a fraud.

subtype: Approach: adjusting the goal after a shortfall [Revision]
passage: I'm Himani. My goal was a set of proper art pens, and I had a chart, a tin and a date. Then March happened: a school project that needed materials, a class trip fee, and a broken geometry set. The tin lost most of a month. I sat on my bed staring at the chart, and the thought crept in: what's the point? My cousin Trisha said, “You don't have to quit, just move the finish line.” So I pushed the target date four weeks later and put a little less into the tin each week, so it wouldn't squeeze me on top of everything else. It felt like a small defeat at first. But the tin started filling again, slowly, and I liked that I hadn't torn up the chart.

qa.q: By how many weeks did Himani move the target date?
qa.a: Himani pushed the target date four weeks later.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when staring at the chart?
qa.a: Himani felt discouraged, since the thought crept in: what's the point?

qa.q: What could Himani try to speed up saving again?
qa.a: Himani could earn a little through small honest work or trim one spending area, since the plan stays while income or costs shift.

qa.q: How might Trisha see Himani's changed plan?
qa.a: Trisha probably feels relieved and glad, since the advice to move the finish line helped Himani keep going.

grounding: After unexpected school expenses, a student extends the target date by four weeks and lowers the weekly amount instead of abandoning the plan.

subtype: Approach: splitting money into save, spend and give [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday. Rukmini spread her 600 rupees on the bed in three piles. “Half for the guitar fund,” she told her brother Sumit, dropping 300 into the tin. “A third for me. That's 200. The rest for Amma's birthday and the temple box.” “Seems fair,” Sumit said. “Can I get a share?” “Only from the gift pile.”
Friday, two weeks on. At the school fair Rukmini bought a bracelet for 60 rupees and felt no guilt at all; that pile was hers to spend.
A month later, on a Sunday, she opened the tin. It held 300 rupees, and the gift envelope's 100 bought a scarf for Amma and rice for the temple kitchen. Nothing felt taken away.

qa.q: How much did Rukmini put into the tin on the first Sunday?
qa.a: Rukmini dropped 300 rupees into the tin.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel about buying the bracelet at the fair?
qa.a: She felt comfortable and free of guilt, since that pile was hers to spend.

qa.q: What could Rukmini do if her allowance goes up or down?
qa.a: She could keep the same shares, half, a third and the rest, and recalculate the amounts, since the plan stays fair as the numbers change.

qa.q: How might Sumit see the plan?
qa.a: Sumit sees it as fair and asks for a share of the gift pile, so he seems interested and perhaps hopes for a present.

grounding: A teen splits money into half for the goal, a third for spending and the rest for gifts or charity, so the plan feels fair.
